title: Invitation, not instruction
hook: Arjuna's bow slips from his hands; after the whole Gita, Krishna says: reflect, then do as you choose
tomorrow: what did a man say when he woke up on a stone pillow?

segments.voice: Ananda began each teaching with its home: thus have I heard. Name the home. Today, how to hand a practice on, once you know where it's from.
screen: `NAME THE HOME.` → `THEN, HOW TO HAND IT ON.`

segments.voice: Two notes on the fridge. One says: pizza night, come if you like. The other says: take out the trash. Same kitchen, a different weight in your hands. The Bhagavad Gita opens with sound: conch shells blown across a battlefield, Krishna's among them. Then a weight. The warrior Arjuna looks across at the other army, sees his own teachers and cousins, and his bow slips from his hands. He sinks down in his chariot. His charioteer is Krishna, who in the Gita is God. What follows is the whole teaching. But listen for how it ends.
screen: `COME IF YOU LIKE, OR DO IT.` → `CONCH SHELLS ACROSS THE FIELD.` → `THE BOW SLIPS FROM HIS HANDS.`

segments.voice: Krishna teaches chapter after chapter: on duty, on the self that doesn't die, on acting without clinging to results, on devotion. He even shows Arjuna his cosmic form. And then, near the end, after all of it, God says something surprising. I have told you this wisdom. Reflect on it fully, and then do as you choose. In Sanskrit, yathecchasi tatha kuru. Not obey. Not because I said so. In this scripture, God hands the choice back. And Arjuna answers that his confusion is gone and he will do as Krishna says. The bow he let fall in the first chapter is his to take up again, by his own yes. He speaks once more after that, a last word of love and refuge, but the choice has already been handed back. Here the teaching is offered in full, reflected on, then chosen. A practice that's forced stays the teacher's. A practice that's chosen becomes yours. So an invitation isn't a weaker kind of instruction. In this verse of the Gita, it's how God offers the whole teaching. Which matters when you're the one passing a practice on: offer it whole, warmly, and leave the hands free to pick it up.
screen: `THE WHOLE TEACHING, OFFERED.` · `REFLECT, THEN DO AS YOU CHOOSE.` · `ARJUNA'S YES IS HIS OWN.` · `CHOSEN, IT BECOMES YOURS.` · then, large: `AN INVITATION.`

segments.voice: Pick up something with a little weight: a book, a mug, your phone. Feel it in your hands, then set it down and let your hands rest open for a few breaths. When you're ready, pick it up again, slowly, because you choose to, and notice how the same weight feels when it's yours.
Invitation: a practice offered whole and warmly, with the choice left in the other person's hands, the way the Gita ends.
Here's the line: an invitation, offered whole, the choice left free, the way Arjuna's yes was his own. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita, whose teaching ends with Krishna telling Arjuna to reflect fully and then choose; people who borrow it offer a practice and leave the choice free.

fork.setup: your partner wants you both to start meditating and has already booked you into a 6 a.m. class. you're annoyed. what fits Gita 18.63?

fork.reveal: Krishna taught at length, then said: reflect on it fully, and do as you choose. Arjuna's yes was his own.

original.note: Sanskrit: do as you choose, Krishna's words to Arjuna near the end of the Bhagavad Gita (18.63).

trapdoor: what you thought: a spiritual teacher tells you what to do.
what it means: in the Gita, even God's long teaching ends by handing the choice back: reflect, then do as you choose.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavad Gita 18.63, 'vimrishyaitad asheshena yathecchasi tatha kuru'; the bow dropped in 1.47; Arjuna's answer in 18.73.

chat.meaning: After teaching Arjuna the whole Gita, Krishna said: reflect on it fully, then do as you choose. A practice is offered, not forced.

tie.story: After the whole Gita, Krishna told Arjuna to reflect fully and do as he chose; Arjuna answered that he would.

Bhagavad Gita.meaning: a Hindu scripture: Krishna's teaching to Arjuna before a battle

Arjuna.meaning: the warrior prince whom Krishna teaches in the Gita

Krishna.meaning: in the Gita, God, serving as Arjuna's charioteer

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.12-19 (the conches), 1.29-30 (the bow Gandiva slips from his hand), 1.47 (Arjuna sinks down, casting away bow and arrows)
Bhagavad Gita 18.63 (reflect on this fully, then do as you wish) and 18.73 (Arjuna: my delusion is gone; I will do your word)

notes: 2026-10-15 v3: written new in recipe v3, shape senses (the conches' sound; the bow's weight dropped and picked up; the practice sets an object down and picks it up by choice). Story: Arjuna's bow slips (Gita 1.47); after the teaching Krishna says 'reflect fully, then do as you choose' (18.63); Arjuna answers (18.73). Teaching named: in the Gita the teaching is offered whole and then chosen.

Check: verse numbers (1.47 is 1.46 in some editions); 'Krishna, who in the Gita is God' (the text's own claim, e.g. ch. 10-11); 'he picks up the bow himself' is implied by 18.73 rather than narrated: a Hindu reviewer should confirm the phrasing. For parents: the setting is a battlefield; nothing violent is described.
'In the Gita, it's the form the whole teaching takes at its close' is a reading of 18.63; confirm it reads as a reading, not a claim about all of Hinduism.

2026-10-15 audit (serious): the teach called 18.63 the 'very end' and 'the form the whole teaching takes at its close'; Krishna speaks again after it (18.64-66, the 'supreme word' of refuge, which many Hindu readers hold to be the culmination). Now says 'near the end', notes he speaks once more, and scopes the claim to this verse. Also: the bow 'slipping' is Gita 1.29/1.30 (gandivam sramsate hastat); 1.47 is where he casts it aside. Myth reveal and chat no longer say Krishna 'ended' with 18.63.
